slurry application rates of up to 50 m3 ha(-1) (equivalent to 2.5 t/ha of solids) do not result in significant losses of P in surface run-off, but that higher rates are likely to increase P losses, particularly when the soil has a propensity to seal.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, whilst there is little evidence to suggest that the application of slurry to land at the rates and frequency recommended in the UK's 'good agricultural practice' guidelines would cause any significant increase in the loss of N and P to surface water via surface run-off, there are circumstances in which such an increase could occur.

the application of cattle slurry at rates of 50 m3 ha(-1) or greater, to silty clay loams, may be expected to result in increased P losses in surface run-off, and the potential for eutrophication of enclosed water bodies.

the application of cattle slurry to land can increase the risk of diffuse pollution of surface waters with NO3(-)- N and P by surface run-off, but that this risk can be reduced to acceptable levels by limiting application rates to those recommended in good agricultural practice guidelines.
The main takeaway from our work is that

slurry applications to arable land, even at rates below those considered agronomically optimal, can cause surface run-off of soluble and total phosphorus, with potentially significant implications for the eutrophication of sensitive catchments.
, whilst losses of P from organic manures via surface run-off are relatively small, the potential for significant pollution in sensitive catchments exists.
